subChunks.title: Electromagnetism — Fields, Circuits & Induction

storyBeats.txt: In 1820, Theodora said, Hans Christian Ørsted noticed that a compass needle deflected when he passed a current through a nearby wire. In that moment, electricity and magnetism — long thought to be separate phenomena — became one subject. A decade later, Faraday showed the reverse: a changing magnetic field produces an electric current.

Maxwell unified all of this in four equations in 1865. From those four equations — written on a single page — follow all of classical electromagnetism, the speed of light, the existence of radio waves, the principles of every electric motor and generator ever built.

Electromagnetism is not just physics — it is the science of nearly all modern technology. Every screen you look at. Every signal your phone receives. The electric grid that powers every building around you. Understanding it is understanding the substrate of modern life.

subChunks.hookHtml: Electromagnetism is one of the four fundamental forces of nature and the basis of all modern electrical technology. Electric fields arise from charge; magnetic fields arise from moving charge; and changing electric and magnetic fields generate each other — a unification first achieved mathematically by James Clerk Maxwell in 1865, whose equations predicted the existence of radio waves two decades before Hertz detected them.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Electric Charge and Coulomb's Law

Electric charge comes in two types: positive and negative. Like charges repel; opposite charges attract. The force between two point charges is given by Coulomb's Law: F = kq₁q₂/r², where k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²·C⁻² (Coulomb's constant) and r is the distance between charges. Structurally identical to Newton's gravitational law but ~10³⁶ times stronger.

The SI unit of charge is the coulomb (C). The elementary charge: e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (charge of a proton or electron). The electric field E at a point is defined as the force per unit positive charge: E = F/q (N/C or V/m).

Electric Circuits

Current (I): Flow of charge. I = ΔQ/Δt. Units: amperes (A = C/s). Conventional current flows from + to −; electron flow is opposite.

Potential difference / Voltage (V): Energy per unit charge. V = W/Q. Units: volts (V = J/C). The electromotive force (EMF) of a source is the energy per unit charge it supplies.

Resistance (R): Opposition to current flow. Units: ohms (Ω).

Ohm's Law: For ohmic conductors (at constant temperature): V = IR. The resistance of a wire: R = ρL/A, where ρ is resistivity (material property), L is length, A is cross-sectional area.

Power: P = IV = I²R = V²/R. Units: watts (W).

Series circuits: Resistors in series: R_total = R₁ + R₂ + ... Current same through all; voltage divides.

Parallel circuits: Resistors in parallel: 1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ... Voltage same across all; current divides.

Kirchhoff's Laws: (1) Loop Law — the sum of EMFs around any closed loop equals the sum of potential drops (energy conservation). (2) Junction Law — the sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum leaving (charge conservation).

Magnetic Fields

Moving charges (currents) produce magnetic fields. A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field experiences a force: F = BIL sin(θ), where B is flux density (Tesla), I is current, L is length, θ is angle between wire and field. The direction is given by Fleming's left-hand rule (for motors): thuMb = Motion, First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current.

A charge moving through a magnetic field: F = qvB sin(θ). This force is always perpendicular to velocity — it does no work and causes circular/helical motion (basis of mass spectrometers and particle accelerators).

Electromagnetic Induction

Faraday's Law: EMF induced in a circuit = −rate of change of magnetic flux. EMF = −dΦ/dt, where Φ = BA cos(θ) is magnetic flux. A changing magnetic field (or a conductor moving through a field) induces an EMF.

Lenz's Law: The induced current flows in a direction such that it opposes the change causing it (a consequence of energy conservation). This is the negative sign in Faraday's Law.

Applications: electric generators (rotation of coil in magnetic field generates alternating EMF); transformers (changing current in primary coil induces EMF in secondary coil — only work with AC); induction heating; wireless phone charging.

Transformer equation: V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p (secondary voltage / primary voltage = secondary turns / primary turns). For ideal transformer: P_in = P_out → V_p I_p = V_s I_s.

Maxwell's Equations and Electromagnetic Waves

James Clerk Maxwell (1865) unified electricity and magnetism in four equations (in differential form): Gauss's Law (electric), Gauss's Law for magnetism, Faraday's Law, and Ampère-Maxwell Law. From these, he derived that changing electric and magnetic fields propagate as a transverse wave at speed c = 1/√(ε₀μ₀) = 3 × 10⁸ m/s — exactly the speed of light. This proved that light is an electromagnetic wave.

Hertz confirmed in 1887 by generating and detecting radio waves. The electromagnetic spectrum — from gamma rays to radio — all follows Maxwell's equations.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old how a transformer works — why power lines carry electricity at very high voltage, and how it gets converted to safe mains voltage at your home.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: A simple circuit has a 12 V battery with internal resistance 1 Ω connected to two resistors: R₁ = 3 Ω in series with a parallel combination of R₂ = 4 Ω and R₃ = 12 Ω. (1) Calculate the equivalent resistance of R₂ and R₃ in parallel. (2) Calculate the total circuit resistance (including internal resistance). (3) Calculate the current drawn from the battery. (4) Calculate the terminal voltage of the battery (voltage across its terminals when delivering current). (5) Calculate the power dissipated in R₁.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) Parallel combination: 1/R₂₃ = 1/4 + 1/12 = 3/12 + 1/12 = 4/12 = 1/3. R₂₃ = 3 Ω.

(2) Total resistance = internal resistance + R₁ + R₂₃ = 1 + 3 + 3 = 7 Ω.

(3) Current I = V/R_total = 12/7 = 1.714 A ≈ 1.71 A.

(4) Terminal voltage = EMF − I × r_internal = 12 − 1.714 × 1 = 10.286 V ≈ 10.3 V. (The internal resistance drops 1.714 V, leaving 10.286 V across the external circuit.)

(5) Power in R₁ = I²R₁ = (1.714)² × 3 = 2.938 × 3 = 8.81 W. Alternatively: voltage across R₁ = IR₁ = 1.714 × 3 = 5.14 V; P = V²/R = (5.14)²/3 = 26.4/3 = 8.81 W. ✓
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: A step-up transformer at a power station outputs 400 kV from a 25 kV generator. (1) Calculate the turns ratio (N_s/N_p). (2) If the generator supplies 500 MW of power, calculate the current in the high-voltage transmission line. (3) The transmission line has a total resistance of 20 Ω. Calculate the power dissipated as heat in the line. (4) Why is high-voltage transmission so much more efficient than low-voltage transmission? Use the formula P_loss = I²R to explain. (5) At the consumer end, a step-down transformer reduces 400 kV to 230 V (mains). How many turns does the secondary coil have if the primary has 200,000 turns?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1) Turns ratio N_s/N_p = V_s/V_p = 400,000/25,000 = 16. The secondary coil has 16 times as many turns as the primary.

(2) P = V_s × I_s → I_s = P/V_s = 500×10⁶ / 400×10³ = 1,250 A.

(3) P_loss = I²R = (1250)² × 20 = 1,562,500 × 20 = 31.25 × 10⁶ W = 31.25 MW. This is 31.25/500 = 6.25% of the transmitted power lost as heat — significant but much less than the alternative.

(4) If the same 500 MW were transmitted at 25 kV (no step-up): I = P/V = 500×10⁶/25,000 = 20,000 A. P_loss = I²R = (20,000)²×20 = 8×10⁹ W = 8,000 MW — vastly more than the total power generated. Transmitting at low voltage is thermodynamically impossible at this scale. The key insight: for a given power P = VI, doubling voltage halves current; since P_loss = I²R, halving current reduces line losses by a factor of 4. Stepping up voltage by 16× reduces current by 16× and reduces line losses by 16² = 256×. High-voltage transmission makes the grid economically viable.

(5) N_s/N_p = V_s/V_p = 230/400,000. N_s = N_p × (230/400,000) = 200,000 × 0.000575 = 115 turns. The step-down transformer has 115 turns in its secondary coil.
learningObjectives: Apply Ohm's Law, Kirchhoff's Laws, and series/parallel resistance rules to analyse DC circuits.
Describe how a magnetic field exerts force on a current-carrying conductor and a moving charge, with reference to Fleming's left-hand rule.
State Faraday's Law and Lenz's Law and explain how they govern electromagnetic induction in generators and transformers.
Explain why Maxwell's equations predict electromagnetic waves at the speed of light and why this proved light is electromagnetic.
commonMistakes: Confusing current and voltage in series vs parallel circuits — in series, current is the same through all components; in parallel, voltage is the same across all components.
Forgetting internal resistance reduces terminal voltage — the terminal voltage of a battery under load is always less than its EMF.
Applying transformer equations to DC — transformers only work with AC; a steady DC in the primary produces no change in flux and therefore no induced EMF in the secondary.
Thinking the magnetic force does work on a moving charge — F = qvB is always perpendicular to velocity, so it does no work and cannot change the speed (only the direction) of the charge.
assessmentCriteria: Correctly calculates equivalent resistance for series and parallel combinations and finds current/voltage/power for each component.
Applies Faraday's Law quantitatively to calculate induced EMF from a given rate of flux change.
Uses transformer equations to calculate turns ratios, voltages, and currents, and explains efficiency losses in power transmission.
Explains why electromagnetic waves travel at c and what Maxwell's equations unify.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Four partial differential equations (1865) unifying electricity and magnetism: Gauss's Law, Gauss's Law for magnetism, Faraday's Law, and Ampère-Maxwell Law. They predict electromagnetic waves at c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s — proving light is electromagnetic.
The induced EMF in a circuit equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux through it: EMF = −dΦ/dt. The foundation of all electrical generators, transformers, and induction devices.

The induced current always flows in a direction that opposes the change in flux that created it — a consequence of energy conservation; explains why generators require mechanical effort to drive against the opposing magnetic force.

At high frequencies (AC), current tends to flow near the surface of conductors rather than through the bulk — effective resistance increases. This is why power lines use bundled conductors and why RF cables have thick outer conductors.

When current flows through a conductor in a magnetic field, a voltage develops perpendicular to both — used in Hall effect sensors to measure magnetic fields, current (contactless), and in the discovery that charge carriers in semiconductors can be positive (holes).

questions.questionHtml: A 6 Ω and a 12 Ω resistor are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery (assume zero internal resistance). What is the total current drawn from the battery?
questions.explanationHtml: In parallel: voltage across each = 12 V. Current through 6 Ω: I₁ = 12/6 = 2 A. Current through 12 Ω: I₂ = 12/12 = 1 A. Total current = 2 + 1 = 3 A. Alternatively: 1/R_total = 1/6 + 1/12 = 2/12 + 1/12 = 3/12, so R_total = 4 Ω. I = V/R = 12/4 = 3 A.

questions.questionHtml: A generator coil rotates at 50 Hz in a magnetic field, producing an AC EMF. The same coil is then rotated at 100 Hz. What happens to the maximum EMF?
options: It halves — faster rotation gives less time for flux to build up
It stays the same — EMF depends only on the magnetic field strength
It doubles — EMF = −dΦ/dt; doubling the frequency doubles the rate of flux change and therefore doubles the peak EMF
It quadruples — because power is proportional to frequency squared
questions.correctAnswer: It doubles — EMF = −dΦ/dt; doubling the frequency doubles the rate of flux change and therefore doubles the peak EMF
questions.explanationHtml: By Faraday's Law, EMF = −dΦ/dt. For a rotating coil, Φ = BAcos(ωt), so EMF = BAω sin(ωt), giving peak EMF = BAω. Since ω = 2πf, doubling frequency doubles ω and therefore doubles peak EMF. The same effect explains why generators at 60 Hz (USA) produce slightly higher peak voltage than those at 50 Hz (UK/Europe) for the same coil geometry — the higher frequency increases the rate of flux change.

questions.questionHtml: A magnet is moved toward a coil of wire, inducing a current. When the magnet is moved faster, the induced current is larger. By Lenz's Law, the coil opposes the approaching magnet. Does this mean you can get energy from the magnet for free? Explain.
options: Yes — the magnetic field provides free energy as kinetic energy of electrons in the coil

No — Lenz's Law means the induced current creates a force opposing the magnet's motion. You must do work to move the magnet against this opposing force — this work is converted to electrical energy in the coil. Energy is conserved.
No — the induced current consumes the magnet's magnetic energy, which is eventually used up
Yes — but only if the coil resistance is zero (superconductor)
questions.correctAnswer: No — Lenz's Law means the induced current creates a force opposing the magnet's motion. You must do work to move the magnet against this opposing force — this work is converted to electrical energy in the coil. Energy is conserved.
questions.explanationHtml: This is the key insight: Lenz's Law is a statement of energy conservation. The induced current's magnetic field opposes the incoming magnet (repels it if approaching) — you must exert a force against this opposition to keep moving the magnet. The work you do (F × distance) equals the electrical energy dissipated in the coil resistance. No energy is created; the magnet's kinetic energy (or the energy you supply) is converted to electrical energy. This is why generators require mechanical input (from turbines, engines, or wind) — without an energy source, induction cannot produce sustained power.
